The verb does change after he, she and it. In my example, "walk" becomes "walks": the verb takes an -s ending because the subject is one person.

Right: My manager writes emails every morning.
Wrong: My manager write emails every morning.

Now try a new one on your own. Write the correct form of the verb:
"Our driver ___ (open) the office door at eight."

Answer with only the verb.
s2001_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=INCORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=NEW_ITEM]]
In my example, "usually" comes before the verb "drinks". Frequency words such as always, usually, sometimes and never go before the main verb, not after it and not at the end.

Right: She always gets up early.
Wrong: She gets up always.

Now try a new one on your own. Rewrite this sentence and add the word "sometimes" in the correct place:
"My cousin plays chess on Sundays."
s2002_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=CORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM criteria=1 next=NEW_ITEM]]
Yes: "is carrying" is the verb group. It has two parts, a form of be and the verb with -ing. That answers my question.

Now write one sentence of your own about a person you know. Say what that person is doing right now.
s2003_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=INCORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=NEW_ITEM]]
After "did", the main verb stays in its base form. In "Did you travel by train?", the word "did" already shows the past, so "travel" does not change.

Right: Did she visit her aunt?
Wrong: Did she visited her aunt?

Now try a new one on your own. Complete the question with the correct form of the verb:
"Did your manager ___ (call) you yesterday?"

Answer with only the verb.
s2004_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=INCORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=SAME_ITEM]]
You wrote that there is no word before "going to". Let us try a smaller step with a different example. Here are two sentences about plans:

"We are going to leave soon."
"We going to leave soon."

One of them follows the English rule for "going to" and one does not. The rule is that "going to" needs a form of the verb be in front of it.

Look at both sentences. Which one is correct English, and which word makes the difference?
s2005_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=INCORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=SAME_ITEM]]
Let us use a general rule to check your choice. We use "How many" for things we can count one by one. We use "How much" for things we do not count.

Now look at my two things again: apples and milk. Think about which one you can count one by one.

Which one would you ask about with "How many"? Tell me in a few words why. Then write one thing in your own kitchen that you can count.
s2006_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=INCORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=NEW_ITEM]]
The word after "faster" is "than". Also, the comparative of a short adjective is made by adding -er to the whole word, so "fast" becomes "faster". No vowels are dropped or changed.

Right: This road is longer than that one.
Wrong: This road is lngr than that one.

Now try a new one on your own. Complete the sentence with the correct form of the adjective:
"My bag is ___ (light) than your bag."

[[assess verdict=CORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=NEW_ITEM]]
Yes: "a" comes before "sandwich", because you can count one sandwich.

Now write one sentence of your own about a person you know who is ordering something in a cafe. Use "Can I have ..., please?" or "I'd like ..." in your sentence.
s2008_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=INCORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=NEW_ITEM]]
The word that gives the reason is "because". In "I am tired because I worked late", the second part explains why the first part is true. We choose the linking word by the meaning, not only by habit.

Right: He is sad because his team lost.
Wrong: He is sad and his team lost.

Now try a new one on your own. Join these two sentences with "because":
"We stayed at home. It was very cold."
s2009_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=INCORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=NEW_ITEM]]
The verb does need to change. In "On Saturday I cleaned my flat", the time word "On Saturday" helps, but the finished action is also shown by the verb ending: "clean" becomes "cleaned" with -ed.

Right: Yesterday we cooked dinner.
Wrong: Yesterday we cook dinner.

Now try a new one on your own. Write the correct past form of the verb:
"Last night I ___ (wash) the car."

Answer with only the verb.
s2010_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=INCORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=NEW_ITEM]]
"Can I have a key, please?" sounds more polite. Reason: it is a question, and it has "please". "Give me a key" is a bare command, and "I want" also sounds too direct when you speak to staff you do not know.

Right: Can I have a towel, please?
Wrong: Give me a towel.

Now try a new one on your own. Make this request polite:
"Give me the menu."
s2011_P2_r1:
[[assess verdict=INCORRECT relevance=ACTIVE_ITEM next=SAME_ITEM]]
Thank you for explaining your idea. It is a common one: many learners think every past verb takes -ed. In English, many common verbs are irregular. They have their own past form, which you learn separately, and they do not take -ed.

For example, "buy" becomes "bought", not "buyed".

Now look at your sentence again: "Last week I seed my friend." Think about whether "see" could be an irregular verb, and write the sentence again.
